title: Let's Learn English
author: VOA Learning English
description: A short, real beginner conversation for practicing greetings, names, and spelling.
levelReason: Short sentences, everyday greetings, clear turn-taking, and repeated names
learningGoal: Introduce yourself, greet someone, and spell a name in a short conversation.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Hi! Are you Anna?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Yes! Hi there! Are you Pete?

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: I am Pete.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Nice to meet you.

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: Let's try that again. I'm Anna. Nice to meet you.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: I'm Pete. Anna — is that A-N-A?

transcript.speaker: Anna
transcript.text: No. A-N-N-A.

transcript.speaker: Pete
transcript.text: Well, Anna with two n's — welcome!

vocabulary.meaning: A friendly, informal way to say hello.
vocabulary.example: Hi there! Are you new here?

vocabulary.meaning: A polite phrase used when meeting someone for the first time.
vocabulary.example: I am Mia. Nice to meet you.

vocabulary.meaning: Do something one more time.
vocabulary.example: Let's try again more slowly.

vocabulary.meaning: To greet someone kindly when they arrive.
vocabulary.example: We welcome new students to the class.

questions.prompt: Who is new to the building?
How many letter N’s are in Anna’s name?
Which phrase do they use when they first meet?

title: How I Built This
author: NPR
episode: Building with purpose, not just momentum
description: Founders unpack the decisions, doubts, and lucky breaks behind remarkable companies.
levelReason: Clear storytelling with some business vocabulary
learningGoal: Follow a founder’s story and notice how past events are connected.

transcript.text: Every company begins with an idea, but ideas rarely arrive fully formed.
For today’s founder, the turning point came when customers started using the product in an unexpected way.
Instead of resisting that change, the team listened carefully and adjusted its plans.
That decision did not guarantee success, but it gave the company a clearer sense of purpose.

vocabulary.meaning: A moment when an important change happens.
vocabulary.example: Customer feedback became a turning point for the company.

vocabulary.meaning: Complete and clearly developed.
vocabulary.example: The plan was not fully formed at the beginning.

vocabulary.meaning: To oppose or avoid accepting something.
vocabulary.example: The team did not resist the new direction.

vocabulary.meaning: The main reason for doing something.
vocabulary.example: The founders shared a strong sense of purpose.

questions.prompt: What caused the company to change direction?

title: Hidden Brain
author: Hidden Brain Media
episode: The curious science of better conversations
description: Stories and science reveal the unconscious patterns that drive human behavior.
levelReason: Measured pace, short sentences, familiar examples
learningGoal: Listen for the main idea and learn phrases for thoughtful conversations.

transcript.text: Have you ever walked away from a conversation and wondered what just happened?
Today, we are going to explore a simple idea: better conversations begin with curiosity.
When we ask a good question, we show another person that we want to understand them.
We also give ourselves time to listen instead of planning our next answer.
This small habit can make an everyday conversation feel more open and honest.

vocabulary.meaning: A strong wish to know or learn something.
vocabulary.example: She asked the question with real curiosity.

vocabulary.meaning: To think about something because you want to know the answer.
vocabulary.example: I wonder why he changed his mind.

vocabulary.meaning: In place of someone or something.
vocabulary.example: Listen instead of planning your reply.

vocabulary.meaning: Truthful and sincere.
vocabulary.example: They had an honest conversation.

questions.prompt: What is the episode’s main idea?
What does a good question show?

title: 99% Invisible
author: Roman Mars
episode: The quiet objects that shape a city
description: A beautifully produced look at the unnoticed architecture and design around us.
levelReason: Natural speech with visual, concrete explanations
learningGoal: Use descriptive language to explain how everyday objects affect people.

transcript.text: Most of us pass hundreds of designed objects before we reach work each morning.
A bench, a sign, or even the edge of a sidewalk quietly tells us how to move through the city.
Good design can feel invisible because it removes a problem before we notice it.
But when a small object fails, the entire street can suddenly feel confusing.

vocabulary.meaning: A path beside a road for people walking.
vocabulary.example: The new sidewalk is wider and safer.

vocabulary.meaning: Impossible or difficult to see.
vocabulary.example: The best design can feel invisible.

vocabulary.meaning: To take something away.
vocabulary.example: The sign removes confusion.

vocabulary.meaning: Whole or complete.
vocabulary.example: The entire street was redesigned.

questions.prompt: Why can good design feel invisible?

title: Search Engine
author: PJ Vogt
episode: A question about the internet we forgot to ask
description: Questions that keep you up at night, investigated with curiosity and wit.
levelReason: Fast dialogue, idioms, and abstract arguments
learningGoal: Track competing arguments and recognize informal idiomatic language.

transcript.text: The internet promised frictionless access to information, but friction may have been doing more work than we realized.
When every answer appears instantaneously, the process of deciding which questions matter can atrophy.
That sounds melodramatic, yet it points to a genuine tension between convenience and judgment.
The technology is not neutral, but neither is our habit of blaming it for choices we willingly make.

vocabulary.meaning: Easy and without obstacles or delay.
vocabulary.example: The service promises a frictionless experience.

vocabulary.meaning: To become weaker from lack of use.
vocabulary.example: Critical skills may atrophy without practice.

vocabulary.meaning: Showing emotions in an exaggerated way.
vocabulary.example: The claim sounds melodramatic at first.

vocabulary.meaning: Not supporting any side or producing a particular effect.
vocabulary.example: The speaker argues that technology is not neutral.

questions.prompt: What may weaken when answers are instant?
options: Our ability to choose meaningful questions

questions.prompt: What tension does the speaker identify?

title: Ologies
author: Alie Ward
description: Ask smart people delightfully curious questions about what they know best.
levelReason: Friendly explanations and repeated key terms
learningGoal: Understand a simple scientific explanation and identify examples.

transcript.text: Today we are looking at a world that is too small for our eyes to see.
Tiny living things are everywhere: in water, in soil, and even inside us.
Most of them do not make us sick. In fact, many help keep our bodies healthy.
Scientists use special tools to study how these small communities live together.

vocabulary.meaning: Very small.
vocabulary.example: A tiny drop of water can contain many organisms.

vocabulary.meaning: The earth where plants grow.
vocabulary.example: Many tiny organisms live in soil.

vocabulary.meaning: Used to add true and often surprising information.
vocabulary.example: Most are harmless. In fact, many are helpful.

vocabulary.meaning: A group living together or sharing something.
vocabulary.example: The organisms form a small community.

questions.prompt: Where can tiny living things be found?
options: In many places, including our bodies

title: Articles of Interest
author: Avery Trufelman
episode: What our clothes say before we do
description: A show about what we wear and the systems, history, and meaning stitched inside.
levelReason: Cultural nuance, complex sentences, and idioms
learningGoal: Interpret implied meaning and discuss how clothing communicates identity.

transcript.text: Clothing speaks on our behalf long before we have the chance to introduce ourselves.
A uniform can signal authority, belonging, resistance, or some unstable combination of all three.
Those meanings are not stitched permanently into the fabric; culture continually renegotiates them.
What appears to be an individual choice is often entangled with class, labor, geography, and aspiration.

vocabulary.meaning: As a representative of someone or something.
vocabulary.example: The uniform speaks on behalf of the organization.

vocabulary.meaning: To communicate information indirectly.
vocabulary.example: Clothing can signal belonging.

vocabulary.meaning: To discuss or define something again under new conditions.
vocabulary.example: Culture renegotiates the meaning of fashion.

vocabulary.meaning: Closely connected in a complicated way.
vocabulary.example: Style is entangled with social identity.

questions.prompt: How does culture affect clothing meanings?
